Adult Amur sturgeon Acipenser schrenckii are among the largest freshwater fishes in Eurasia, with an ultimate total length of 346 centimeters [Li = 346 centimeters] recorded in the lower Amur River basin. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty is typically 133 centimeters [Lp = 133 centimeters], though regional variability is evident; some populations exhibit maturation at lengths ranging from 125 to 143 centimeters. These large-bodied acipenserids undergo an extended juvenile phase, accumulating substantial somatic tissue before initiating gonadal development. The impressive maximum size of this species, which rivals that of related sturgeons in the Huso genus, is coupled with a remarkably low initial mass at emergence from the egg. Fertilised ova in this species have a diameter of approximately 3.1 millimeters, yielding a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.0156 grams [Wwb = 0.0156 grams], a value typical of acipenserids with demersal, adhesive eggs that require cool riverine incubation.

At a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum daily reproduction rate of Amur sturgeon reaches approximately 890 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 890 eggs per day]. Females produce a single clutch of approximately 1.3 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1.3 million eggs per spawning event], though spawning intervals are infrequent. Based on observations by Krykhtin and Svirskii in 1997, individual females spawn only once every 4 years [F_R_i = once every 4 years] under natural fluvial conditions, meaning that the effective annual egg production is spread across a very long reproductive lifespan. This iteroparous strategy, combining extreme fecundity per event with widely spaced reproductive bouts, is characteristic of late-maturing, long-lived acipenserids. The energetic investment in each batch of yolky eggs is substantial, and the long interval between spawnings likely reflects the time required to rebuild ovarian reserves after a major reproductive event in the cold, oligotrophic waters of the Amur River system.

Recorded values for the wet weight at puberty in Acipenser schrenckii centre around 13,300 grams [Wwp = around 13,300 grams], although individual variation is considerable; published accounts document a range between 8.3 and 16.4 kilograms for first-time spawners in the middle Amur. This pubertal mass, equivalent to roughly 7 percent of the species ultimate wet weight of 190,000 grams [Wwi = 190,000 grams], reflects the prolonged somatic growth trajectory that precedes reproductive activation. The maximum adult body mass, derived from length-weight relationships using the coefficient 0.00324 and an exponent of 3.17, underscores the considerable size disparity between immature juveniles and fully grown adults. Field-caught specimens exceeding 100 kilograms have been documented, but the average reproductively active individual is considerably smaller, typically attaining masses well below the asymptotic upper bound during the early decades of life.

When maintained at a thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at puberty for Amur sturgeon is approximately 4,380 days [tp = approximately 4,380 days], a value equivalent to 12 years [tp = 12 years] of continuous development. This extended prepubertal period, among the longest recorded for any sturgeon species native to Asian river systems, is consistent with the slow metabolic and growth rates imposed by cool temperate waters. During this protracted juvenile stage, individuals traverse several distinct ontogenetic phases: from yolk-sac larva through the exotrophic transition to active feeding, followed by years as a benthic-foraging juvenile before the onset of gonadal recrudescence. The HPG axis activation that culminates in first spawning is tightly coupled to both size and condition thresholds, and the 12-year benchmark likely represents a minimum estimate under favourable feeding conditions. Regional warming trends or alterations in prey availability could shift this developmental timeline considerably, though empirical data remain scarce for the species.

The maximum lifespan of Amur sturgeon in its native environment, measured at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is estimated at 21,900 days [am = 21,900 days], or roughly 60 years [am = roughly 60 years]. This extraordinary longevity aligns with the life-history syndrome of large, slowly maturing acipenserids that experience negligible natural mortality once they reach adult body sizes exceeding one meter. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with gravid individuals well over 40 years of age still contributing to annual spawning runs in undammed sections of the Amur River. The trade-off between delayed maturity and extended reproductive lifespan is stark: a female that begins spawning at 12 years may participate in more than ten discrete breeding events over her lifetime, each separated by a 4-year interval. Comparative data from related species such as Acipenser baerii and Acipenser ruthenus suggest that the 60-year benchmark is at the upper end of the genus, reflecting the particularly cold, stable thermal environment and low predation pressure on adult sturgeons in the Amur basin.
